figures.label: FIGURE 6-25
figures.title: FIGURE 6-25 The circulatory system includes the heart, arteries, veins, and interconnecting capillaries. The capillaries are the smallest vessels and connect venules and arterioles. At the center of the system, and providing its driving force, is the heart. Blood circulates
figures.description: The superior vena cava, carrying oxygen-poor blood from head and upper body is a large trunk-like vein located toward the right side of the heart. The right pulmonary artery, carrying blood to right lung, and left pulmonary artery, carrying blood to left lung, begin at the base of the heart’s ventricles on either side. The right atrium is located in the right corner of the heart. The inferior vena cava, carrying oxygen-poor blood from lower body, is a large vein that shows below the right atrium. The right ventricle is located in the lower right portion of the heart below the right atrium. The right pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood from the right lung. The left pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood from the left lung. Carbon dioxide from the cells is carried through the venules to the superior vena cava and inferior vena cava and the right atrium, then the left atrium from where it is pumped to the lungs through the Pulmonary arteries. The oxygenated blood is taken from the lungs to the left atrium through pulmonary veins. Then from the left ventricle, it is pumped through the aorta, artery, and arterioles to tissue cells in the upper and lower body.
figures.crossrefs: The  circulatory system  is a complex arrangement of connected tubes, including the arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules, and veins (   ).

figures.label: FIGURE 6-31
figures.title: FIGURE 6-31 Significant blood loss results in reduced stroke volume (SV). To compensate, the body increases heart rate (HR) and systemic vascular resistance to maintain mean arterial pressure (MAP).
figures.description: M A P equals C O times P V R. Mean or average B P equals Cardiac output times Peripheral vascular resistance. Cardiac output equals H R times S V, that is, 80 per minute times 70 milliliters per beat which is 5600 milliliters per minute or 5.6 liters per minute. Mean or average B P equals H R times S V times Peripheral vascular resistance. A massive hemorrhage reduces stroke volume. In order to maintain B P, Vascular resistance and H R must increase.
figures.seen_description: A flow diagram of the blood-pressure equation: MAP = CO x PVR (mean/average BP = cardiac output x peripheral vascular resistance), with CO = HR x SV worked as 80/min x 70 mL/beat = 5,600 mL/min or 5.6 L/min, and arrows showing that when massive hemorrhage reduces stroke volume, heart rate and vascular resistance must increase to maintain BP.

figures.label: FIGURE 6-33
figures.title: FIGURE 6-33 The basic configuration of the nervous system.
figures.description: At the top of the diagram is central nervous system or C N S with brain and spinal cord. Then comes the peripheral nervous system with nerves that connect all parts of the body to the brain and motor division, which is made up of motor fibers that conduct nerve impulses from C N S to muscles and glands. The motor division is divided into two, autonomic nervous system that conducts nerve impulses from C N S to organs and glands and the somatic nervous system that conducts nerve impulses from C N S to muscles; voluntary control. Then comes the sympathetic division that activates body during emergency situations and the parasympathetic division that controls nonemergency functions. The sensory division conducts sensory information from sense organs and other internal organs to C N S through the peripheral nervous system, which has nerves that connect all parts of the body to the brain, that is, the central nervous system or C N S with brain and spinal cord.
figures.crossrefs: The  autonomic nervous system  controls those functions that occur autonomously (ie, automatically), including digestion, dilation and constriction of blood vessels, sweating, and other involuntary actions (   ).
figures.seen_description: A flowchart of nervous-system organization: the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) processing information from the body and commanding it to action, above the peripheral nervous system, which branches into the somatic nervous system controlling voluntary muscles and the autonomic nervous system splitting into parasympathetic (feed or breed) and sympathetic (fight or flight); no brain regions or lobes are labelled.

figures.crossrefs: Three major subdivisions of the brain are the cerebrum, the cerebellum, and the brainstem (   ).
figures.seen_description: A midsagittal cutaway of the head showing the brain inside the skull, with only three labels: cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem.

figures.label: TABLE 6-10
figures.title: TABLE 6-10 Structures of the Nervous System and General Functions
figures.crossrefs: summarizes several key components of the nervous system and their functions.
figures.seen_description: A four-column table (System, Major Structure, Subdivision, General Function) listing the occipital, parietal, temporal and frontal lobes, the prefrontal area, limbic system, thalamus and hypothalamus, then the midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata of the brainstem, the spinal cord, and the cranial and peripheral nerves, each with its general function.

figures.label: FIGURE 6-35
figures.title: FIGURE 6-35 The spinal cord is a continuation of the brainstem. It exits the skull at the foramen magnum and extends down to the level of the second lumbar vertebra.
figures.description: The brain has the cerebrum, cerebellum, and brain stem. The spinal cord extends from the brain stem through foramen magnum at the base of the skull and down the back. There are several spinal nerves on the spinal cord.
figures.crossrefs: Spinal Cord The  spinal cord  is an extension of the brainstem (   ).
figures.seen_description: A posterior view of a man's head and back with the brain and spinal cord drawn in, labelling the cerebrum, cerebellum, brain stem, foramen magnum, spinal cord and the spinal nerves branching off it down to the sacrum.

figures.label: FIGURE 6-36
figures.title: FIGURE 6-36 The layers of the skin can be divided between the epidermis and the dermis. Below the skin is a layer of subcutaneous tissue.
figures.description: The epidermis: The top most layer has Hair and pore, and below that a germinal layer of epidermis. The Dermis: The hair follicle with the sebaceous gland and arrector pili muscle attached to it; sweat gland; blood vessel, and sensory nerves lie in the dermis. Subcutaneous tissue: Subcutaneous fat below the dermis and layers of fascia and muscles lie in the subcutaneous tissue.
figures.crossrefs: Beneath these layers is  subcutaneous tissue  (   ).
figures.seen_description: A block cutaway of skin labelling the epidermis, dermis and subcutaneous tissue, and within them the hair, pore, germinal layer of epidermis, sebaceous gland, arrector pili muscle, sensory nerve, sweat gland, hair follicle, blood vessel, subcutaneous fat, fascia and muscle.

figures.label: FIGURE 6-37
figures.title: FIGURE 6-37 The boundaries of the abdomen are the anterior and posterior abdominal cavity walls, the diaphragm, and an imaginary plane from the pubic symphysis to the sacrum. The region below the plane is called the pelvic cavity. A. Anterior view. B. Lateral view.
figures.description: A: Anterior view. Chest cavity from the base of neck to the diaphragm. The abdominal cavity surrounded by the abdominal wall extends from the diaphragm to the plane from sacrum to pubic symphysis. The horizontal plane is drawn through the sacrum at the base of the spine and pubis at the anterior of the pelvic bone. B: Chest cavity from the base of the neck to the diaphragm. The abdominal cavity surrounded by the abdominal wall extends from the diaphragm to the plane from sacrum to pubic symphysis. The horizontal plane is drawn through the sacrum at the base of the spine and pubis symphysis in a slightly slanted plane. The pelvic cavity lies beneath the plane.
figures.crossrefs: Inferiorly, the abdomen is separated from the pelvis by an imaginary plane that extends from the pubic symphysis through the sacrum (   ).
figures.seen_description: A. an anterior view of the torso and B. a lateral view, each shading the chest cavity and the abdominal cavity and marking the diaphragm, the abdominal wall, the sacrum and pubis, and the tilted plane from sacrum to pubic symphysis, with the pelvic cavity labelled below that plane in B.

figures.label: FIGURE 6-38
figures.title: FIGURE 6-38 A. In the abdomen, quadrants are the easiest system for identifying areas. Major bony landmarks are also shown. B. Several of the organs in the abdomen lie in more than one quadrant.
figures.crossrefs: On the anterior abdominal wall, the quadrants thus formed are the right upper, right lower, left upper, and left lower (   ).
figures.seen_description: A. an anterior torso divided into right and left upper and lower quadrants with the costal arch, umbilicus, iliac crest, anterior superior iliac spine, inguinal ligament and pubic symphysis labelled; B. the same torso with the quadrant lines drawn over the organs - esophagus, diaphragm, stomach, spleen, liver, gallbladder, bile duct, small intestine, appendix, large intestine and rectum.

figures.label: FIGURE 6-39
figures.title: FIGURE 6-39 The major organs of the retroperitoneal space lie behind the abdominal cavity, above the level of the umbilicus, and extend from the 11th rib to the 3rd lumbar vertebra. The bladder, inferior vena cava, and aorta also lie in this space.
figures.description: Both the kidneys with the adrenal gland at their apex, the pancreas and the duodenum between the kidneys; The ureters connecting the kidneys to the urinary bladder; Inferior vena cava and aorta running down the middle of the abdomen are also shown.
figures.crossrefs: The kidneys and pancreas are called  retroperitoneal  organs because they lie behind the abdominal cavity (   ).
figures.seen_description: An anterior torso showing the retroperitoneal organs - both kidneys with an adrenal gland on each, the pancreas and duodenum between them, the ureters running down to the urinary bladder, and the aorta and inferior vena cava.

figures.label: FIGURE 6-40
figures.title: FIGURE 6-40 The endocrine system controls the production and release of hormones in the body.
figures.crossrefs: Endocrine glands release their hormones directly into the bloodstream (   ).
figures.seen_description: A male and a female figure side by side with the endocrine glands drawn in place and labelled: hypothalamus, pineal gland, pituitary, thyroid, parathyroids, thymus, adrenal glands, pancreas, ovaries and testes.

figures.label: FIGURE 6-41
figures.title: FIGURE 6-41 The endocrine system is tightly controlled with primary and secondary feedback loops to keep body systems in balance.
figures.crossrefs: This cycle is known as a feedback loop, and it helps keep the body’s systems and functions in balance (   ).

figures.label: FIGURE 6-42
figures.title: FIGURE 6-42 The urinary system lies in the retroperitoneal (behind the peritoneum) space behind the organs of the digestive system. The urinary system in men and women includes the kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra. This diagram shows the male urinary system.
figures.description: The bean-shaped kidneys are connected to the bladder with long tubes of the ureter. The ureters open into the bladder at the Ureter opening. The Prostate gland lies beneath the bladder with the Urethra passing through it. The Urethra continues down through the penis and ends at the External urethral opening at the tip of the penis.
figures.crossrefs: In the urinary system, the kidneys are solid organs; the ureters, bladder, and urethra are hollow organs (   ).
figures.seen_description: The male urinary tract isolated from the body: both kidneys, the ureters descending to a cutaway bladder showing the ureter openings, and the prostate gland, urethra, penis and external urethral opening.

figures.label: FIGURE 6-43
figures.title: FIGURE 6-43 The male reproductive system consists of the testicles, epididymis, vasa deferentia, prostate gland, seminal vesicles, and penis.
figures.description: Front view: The ureters are connected to the pear-shaped urinary bladder. The testis lies posterior to the bladder on either side. The testes are connected by the Epididymis to the tubular Vasa deferentia, which extend to the urinary bladder. Prostate gland lies beneath the bladder. The urethra passes through the Prostate gland and the penis. The enlarged tip of the penis is labeled Glans penis. Side view: The pubic bone lies between the Urinary bladder and the front abdominal wall. Prostate gland lies between the bladder and the penis. The sac of the scrotum is posterior to the penis with the testis within. Epididymis at the top of the testis connects it to the tube of the Vasa deferentia, which extends to the bladder. Urethra runs down the middle of the penis and prostate gland.
figures.seen_description: The male reproductive organs in front view and side view, labelling the ureter, urinary bladder, vasa deferentia, prostate gland, urethra, epididymis, testis, penis, glans penis, scrotum and pubic bone.

figures.label: FIGURE 6-44
figures.title: FIGURE 6-44 The female reproductive system consists of the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and vagina.
figures.description: Front view: The Uterus is connected to the ovary on either side by the uterine, fallopian tube. Cervix is at the mouth of the uterus and continues down as the vagina. Side view: Uterus with the uterine, fallopian tube running above to the ovary; cervix at the mouth of the uterus facing the posterior abdominal wall; and vagina are shown.
figures.crossrefs: The female reproductive organs include the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and vagina (   ).
figures.seen_description: The female reproductive organs in front view and side view, labelling the ovary, uterine (fallopian) tube, uterus, cervix and vagina.
